report:
## Research Summary

The claim that vegetarian diets increase life expectancy compared with meat-eating is **partially supported but overstated** by current evidence.

**What the evidence shows:**
- A 2021 meta-analysis found vegetarian diets were associated with reduced ischemic heart disease mortality, but had **no significant effect on all-cause mortality** compared with non-vegetarian diets, and the authors rated the certainty of evidence as low (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34611632/).
- The large Adventist Health Study-2 cohort—one of the most-cited sources on this topic—found protective associations between vegetarian diets and all-cause mortality, but this is a religiously and lifestyle-homogeneous population (low smoking/alcohol use) that may not generalize broadly (https://ajcn.nutrition.org/article/S0002-9165(24)00652-X/fulltext).
- The UK-based EPIC-Oxford cohort found **no significant differences** in all-cause, heart disease, or stroke mortality between vegetarians and meat-eaters after ~11 years follow-up, though vegetarians did show lower rates of some cancers (https://veganhealth.org/chronic-disease-and-vegetarian-diets/vegetarian-cohorts/).
- Newer plant-based diet index meta-analyses (2024–2025) suggest that "healthful" plant-based patterns (rich in whole grains, vegetables, legumes) are linked to lower mortality risk, but this is about diet *quality*, not vegetarianism per se—unhealthy plant-based diets (refined carbs, sugar) show no benefit or even harm.

**Key caveat:** Most vegetarian cohorts (Adventist, EPIC-Oxford) show vegetarians and omnivores share similarly low overall mortality compared to national averages, suggesting **healthy-user bias**—vegetarians tend to smoke less, drink less, exercise more, and have higher socioeconomic status—confounds the diet-mortality relationship (https://veganhealth.org/chronic-disease-and-vegetarian-diets/vegetarian-cohorts/).

**Conclusion:** Vegetarian diets appear to modestly reduce risk of specific outcomes (ischemic heart disease, some cancers) but evidence for a broad, robust increase in overall life expectancy versus meat-eating is weak and confounded. Diet quality matters more than strict vegetarianism.
